clinicalPearls: A benign, fluid-filled cyst of the epididymis, usually arising from the head and containing clear serous fluid, in contrast to the sperm-laden fluid of a spermatocele
Presents as a painless, smooth, mobile swelling felt separate from and usually above and behind the testis
Transilluminates brightly, reflecting its clear fluid content
Often multiple and bilateral, and very common as an incidental finding
Scrotal ultrasound confirms a thin-walled anechoic cyst separate from the testis and is the key investigation
The distinction from a spermatocele is largely academic, resting on content rather than behaviour, as both are benign and managed the same way
Most need only reassurance; excision is reserved for large, painful, or bothersome cysts, with counselling about the small risk to fertility from epididymal surgery
reference.pathophysiology: An epididymal cyst arises from cystic dilatation of the epididymal tubules or efferent ductules, probably from obstruction or from embryological ductal remnants, producing a thin-walled sac of clear serous fluid. Unlike a spermatocele, this fluid does not contain spermatozoa. The cysts are lined by flattened epithelium, grow slowly, and are entirely benign with no malignant potential; they become clinically important only when large enough to cause discomfort or anxiety.
additionalDifferentials: Cyst of the appendix testis or appendix epididymis
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination confirming the lump is separate from the testis
Testicular tumour markers if any solid component is seen
Interval review where there is diagnostic uncertainty
redFlags: A solid or vascular component on ultrasound
An associated painful, hard testicular mass
reference.prognosis: Excellent, as epididymal cysts are benign and often remain stable or fluctuate in size; even when excised the outlook is good, with only a small risk to ipsilateral epididymal function.
pitfalls: Excising asymptomatic cysts and risking epididymal obstruction and fertility impairment
Failing to obtain ultrasound to exclude a solid testicular lesion behind a scrotal lump
Confusing an epididymal cyst with a hydrocele or with a spermatocele
Under-counselling younger men about the fertility implications of surgery
management: Reassure and manage conservatively, as epididymal cysts are benign with no malignant potential and often remain stable
Confirm the diagnosis with scrotal ultrasound showing a thin-walled anechoic cyst separate from the testis, with interval review where there is uncertainty
Offer simple analgesia and scrotal support for discomfort
Reserve surgical excision for large or persistently symptomatic cysts, counselling the patient about the small risk to ipsilateral epididymal function and fertility
Investigate any solid component with testicular tumour markers and prompt referral to exclude malignancy
